opportunities.title: Propose vulnerability identity key and lifecycle schema
opportunities.summary: ### Summary Inspect the committed Anchore JSON fixtures and propose a schema for tracking vulnerabilities over time. Specifically: what combination of fields uniquely identifies "the same vulnerability" across scans? Candidates to evaluate include CVE ID alone, CVE + package name, CVE + package name + version, and CVE + package + image. Write up the tradeoffs, pick a recommendation, and sketch the analytics DB table(s) needed to support first_seen / last_seen / fixed_at / ignored_at / cleared_at fields. **Tech notes:** The Anchore JSON schema is documented at the Anchore project site; worth skimming before diving into fixtures. The goal of this spike is a decision, not code — resist the urge to start implementing. ### Acceptance criteria - [ ] Written proposal (markdown doc in PR) covering identity key options, tradeoffs, and a recommendation - [ ] Proposed analytics DB schema with column types and rationale - [ ] At least one worked example from the fixtures showing how the identity key behaves across days - [ ] Reviewed and approved by Brandon and/or Matt before next ticket starts ## Bounty: $250 This issue has been selected for our paid contributor program. opportunities.title: 🎯 Prevent Indefinite Request Throttling When RateLimiter Burst is Configured Too Low
opportunities.summary: ## 📝 Description In `client-go`, the client-side rate limiting is managed via the `util/flowcontrol` package, which wraps `golang.org/x/time/rate`. Currently, if a `RateLimiter` is configured with a very small burst size (specifically `burst <= 0` or a burst size that is too small relative to the concurrency of the requests), requests can be throttled indefinitely. In `golang.org/x/time/rate`, a token bucket with a burst of `0` will never allow any tokens to be consumed, causing `Wait()` or `Accept()` calls to block indefinitely or fail continuously. This issue tracks the implementation of a safeguard to ensure that the rate limiter is never initialized with a burst size that causes indefinite blocking, defaulting to a minimum safe burst size (e.g., `1`) when an invalid or dangerously low burst is provided. ## 🎯 Acceptance Criteria - [ ] `NewTokenBucketRateLimiter(qps float32, burst int)` must automatically sanitize the `burst` parameter. opportunities.title: parse_duration drops the days (d) unit
opportunities.summary: ## Bug `parse_duration` silently drops the **days** (`d`) unit. The README lists `d` as a supported unit, but the parser ignores it and returns a wrong (too-small) result instead of raising or counting it. ### Reproduction ```python from duration_utils import parse_duration parse_duration("1d") # -> 0 (expected 86400) parse_duration("2d4h") # -> 14400 (expected 187200) ``` ### Expected `d` should be counted as 86400 seconds, so `parse_duration("1d") == 86400` and `parse_duration("2d4h") == 187200`. ### Notes The `d` character is already accepted by the token regex, so malformed-input detection still passes — the value is just never added. A fix should add the `d` unit and cover it with tests. /bounty $50

opportunities.title: 🎯 Fail with descriptive error instead of silently sending unauthenticated API requests when keyring access fails
opportunities.summary: ## 📝 Description When executing `gh api` commands, `cli` attempts to resolve authentication tokens for the target host via the configured credential store (such as the system keyring, environment variables, or config files). If credential retrieval from the system keyring fails due to an operational or system error (e.g., locked keychain, missing D-Bus session, OS permission denied, corrupted secret store), the error is swallowed and treated as if no credentials exist. Consequently, `gh api` silently proceeds with an unauthenticated HTTP request.
